Incremental store of the relatedness matrix

Source: R/relstore.R
relstore.Rd

A store is an object that keeps the additive relationship matrix \(A = 2\phi\) among the individuals currently in it, and that is updated as individuals are added and removed. Because relatedness between existing individuals never changes when new individuals are born, a newborn's row is computed once from its parents' rows, at a cost proportional to the number of individuals the store has held at once instead of recomputing the whole matrix. Individuals who can no longer become parents (dead, emigrated, ...) should be removed so that their slots are recycled. The cost per birth and the memory then depend on the number of individuals in the store, not on the length of the pedigree.

Usage

rel_new(remember_removed = c("none", "fingerprint", "id"))

rel_copy(rel)

rel_add(rel, ped)

rel_remove(rel, ids)

rel_get(
  rel,
  ids = rel_ids(rel),
  metric = c("additive", "kinship", "wright", "hamilton", "Wright", "Hamilton")
)

rel_ids(rel)

rel_size(rel)

rel_capacity(rel)

# S3 method for class 'relatedness_store'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

remember_removed

Should the store keep a trace of the individuals removed, so that rel_add() refuses to add them again? "none" (the default) for no trace, "fingerprint" for a compact trace that is wrong with a negligible probability, or "id" for the identifiers themselves, which takes more memory but is never wrong (see the section Removed individuals).

rel

A store created by rel_new().

ped

A data frame (or a tibble) with one row per individual to add and three columns giving the identifier of the individual, of its father and of its mother (NA or 0 for unknown parents). The columns are found by their names (e.g. id, dad, mom or Animal, Sire, Dam), whatever their order, and other columns are ignored: see the section Columns of ped in fastrel_ped(). Only individuals not yet in the store can be added. Known parents must be in the store or in ped itself: any other identifier raises an error rather than being treated as unknown, since it usually reveals a mistake (a typo, a parent never added or removed too early). 0 is taken as an unknown parent unless an individual is called 0, in which case it is refused as ambiguous. The rows of ped may be in any order.

ids

Character vector (or coercible to it) of individual identifiers. A data frame with a single column is taken as that column. For rel_get(), the default is every individual in the store.

metric

The measure of relatedness returned by rel_get(): "additive" (the default), "kinship", "wright" (or "Wright") or "hamilton" (or "Hamilton"). Abbreviations are accepted. See relatedness_metrics. The store always holds the additive relationship, and the conversion is done on the matrix extracted only.

x

A store created by rel_new().

...

Ignored.

Value

rel_new() returns the store. rel_copy() returns a new store, identical to rel (same individuals, slots, capacity and trace of the removed individuals) but independent of it. rel_add() and rel_remove() return the store invisibly. rel_get() returns a matrix with ids as dimnames: with the default metric = "additive", it is symmetric with diagonal 1 + F (see relatedness_metrics for the other measures). rel_ids() returns a character vector, in order of insertion. rel_size() and rel_capacity() return integers.

Details

The functions work as follows:

  • rel_new() creates an empty store.

  • rel_add() adds individuals, given by a data frame with columns for the focal individual, its father and its mother.

  • rel_remove() removes individuals.

  • rel_get() extracts the relatedness matrix among chosen individuals, as any of the measures described in relatedness_metrics.

  • rel_copy() returns an independent copy of a store.

  • rel_ids() lists the individuals in the store.

  • rel_size() and rel_capacity() report the number of individuals in the store and the number of slots allocated.

Vocabulary

Store and slot are everyday words of computer science, not terms of R or of C++.

  • A store is a container that keeps data in memory between calls, here the relatedness matrix. You create it once and then pass it to the other functions, which read it or update it.

  • A slot is one position in the matrix of the store, i.e. one row and the matching column, reserved for one individual. An individual occupies a slot from the moment it is added until it is removed; the slot is then free and is given to an individual added later. The matrix is allocated with more slots than needed so that it does not have to be enlarged at each birth: its number of slots is the capacity of the store.

What a store is made of

The object returned by rel_new() is an R environment (the kind of object created by new.env()) of class "relatedness_store". It holds the identifiers of the individuals, the slot of each of them, and a pointer to a C++ object which holds the matrix itself. Two consequences follow, which differ from the usual behaviour of R objects:

  • Like any R environment, a store is modified in place and is not copied when it is assigned or passed to a function: rel_add() and rel_remove() change the store they are given, and after rel2 <- rel both names refer to the same store. Use rel_copy() to get a store that can be modified without changing the original.

  • The matrix lives in memory managed by C++, outside the memory managed by R. It is therefore not written by save() or saveRDS(), and a store read back from such a file is unusable: use rel_save() and rel_load() instead. For the same reason utils::object.size() does not see it: see the section Memory management.

The content of the environment is internal: use the functions above rather than reading or modifying it directly.

What to keep in the store

Keep an individual for as long as it can still become a parent, or for as long as you want to query its relatedness. A removed individual cannot be used as a parent later (rel_add() raises an error), and a newborn gets no relatedness value with individuals removed before its birth. Relatedness values among the remaining individuals are not affected by removals.

Removal is final. The relatedness between a removed individual and those born afterwards is not tracked, so if it is added again it comes back as unrelated to everybody, which is wrong for its relatives. By default nothing prevents this: it is up to you never to add again an individual that was removed. With rel_new(remember_removed = "fingerprint") or rel_new(remember_removed = "id"), rel_add() raises an error instead (see the section Removed individuals).

Removed individuals

With remember_removed set to "fingerprint" or "id" (rather than "none", the default), the store keeps a trace of every individual removed and rel_add() refuses to add it again. This protects against a silent error, at a cost in memory that grows slowly with the length of the pedigree, instead of depending only on the number of individuals in the store. This is why it is off by default. Two kinds of trace are offered:

  • "fingerprint" keeps a 64-bit fingerprint of each identifier, about 30 bytes per individual removed (30 MB per million). A new identifier can be mistaken for a removed one, but with a negligible probability: the number of individuals removed divided by 2^64, i.e. less than 1 in 10 million millions per addition after a million removals.

  • "id" keeps the identifiers themselves, so it can never be wrong, but it takes more memory, which increases with the length of the identifiers: about 70 bytes per individual removed for identifiers of up to 15 characters, and about 115 bytes for identifiers of 34 characters.

Both add little to the time taken by rel_add() and rel_remove(), "id" a little more than "fingerprint" since it handles whole identifiers. The cost only becomes noticeable when individuals are added and removed in large numbers without much else being computed.

Metapopulations

To follow several patches connected by migration, use a single store for the whole metapopulation and do not remove the individuals that move to another patch: remove them only when they die or leave the metapopulation for good. Keep track of who is in which patch in your simulation, and extract the matrix of a patch with rel_get(rel, ids_of_the_patch). Migrants then keep their exact relatedness with everybody, including the relatives they left behind and the offspring they produce elsewhere. The time per birth and the memory depend on the number of individuals alive over all the patches (see the section Memory management).

Creating the store with rel_new(remember_removed = "fingerprint") or rel_new(remember_removed = "id") is recommended here: with individuals moving between patches, removing one that left a patch and adding it again when it comes back is an easy mistake to make, and it would go unnoticed.

Memory management

The store allocates its matrix by itself: there is nothing to set. The matrix has one row and one column per slot, hence uses 8 * rel_capacity(rel)^2 bytes. When all the slots are taken, the number of slots grows by half (or more if a single call to rel_add() requires it), which costs a one-off copy of the matrix. Beyond the initial 16 slots, the number of slots therefore stays within about 1.5 times the largest number of individuals the store has held at once. It never shrinks.

R does not see this memory: utils::object.size() or lobstr::obj_size() only report the small R side of a store. Also, each time the matrix is enlarged, the old and the new matrix coexist for a moment, and the memory of the old one is not always returned to the operating system at once: in our benchmark, a store that grew in small steps made the R process use about 20% more memory than its matrix. All the figures given here can be checked on your machine with the script system.file("benchmarks/memory_benchmark.R", package = "fastrel").

See also

fastrel_ped() to compute the whole matrix from a pedigree; rel_save() and rel_load() to save a store to disk.

Examples

rel <- rel_new()

## founders: unknown parents
rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = c("A", "B", "C", "D"), dad = NA, mom = NA))

## births: the columns are found by their names, in any order
rel_add(rel, data.frame(sire = c("B", "D"), dam = c("A", "C"), animal = c("E", "F")))
rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = "G", dad = "F", mom = "E"))

## deaths (or emigration): free the slots
rel_remove(rel, c("A", "B", "C", "D"))
rel_size(rel)
#> [1] 3
rel_ids(rel)
#> [1] "E" "F" "G"

## a mother-son mating
rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = "H", dad = "G", mom = "E"))

A <- rel_get(rel)
A
#>      E    F    G    H
#> E 1.00 0.00 0.50 0.75
#> F 0.00 1.00 0.50 0.25
#> G 0.50 0.50 1.00 0.75
#> H 0.75 0.25 0.75 1.25
diag(A) - 1   # inbreeding coefficients
#>    E    F    G    H 
#> 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.25 
rel_get(rel, metric = "kinship")   # other measures: see ?relatedness_metrics
#>       E     F     G     H
#> E 0.500 0.000 0.250 0.375
#> F 0.000 0.500 0.250 0.125
#> G 0.250 0.250 0.500 0.375
#> H 0.375 0.125 0.375 0.625

## an independent copy, e.g. to explore two scenarios from the same state
rel2 <- rel_copy(rel)
rel_remove(rel2, "H")
rel_ids(rel)    # unchanged
#> [1] "E" "F" "G" "H"
rel_ids(rel2)
#> [1] "E" "F" "G"

## two patches: one store, and the patch of each individual kept aside
rel <- rel_new(remember_removed = "id")
rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = c("a1", "a2", "b1", "b2"), dad = NA, mom = NA))
patch <- c(a1 = "A", a2 = "A", b1 = "B", b2 = "B")
rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = "a3", dad = "a2", mom = "a1"))   # born in A
patch["a3"] <- "A"
patch["a3"] <- "B"                                            # a3 moves to B
rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = "b3", dad = "a3", mom = "b1"))   # and breeds there
patch["b3"] <- "B"
rel_get(rel, names(patch)[patch == "B"])
#>     b1 b2  a3  b3
#> b1 1.0  0 0.0 0.5
#> b2 0.0  1 0.0 0.0
#> a3 0.0  0 1.0 0.5
#> b3 0.5  0 0.5 1.0
rel_get(rel)["b3", "a1"]   # b3 is related to its grandparent in patch A
#> [1] 0.25

## with remember_removed = "id", a removed individual cannot come back
rel_remove(rel, "a3")
try(rel_add(rel, data.frame(id = "a3", dad = NA, mom = NA)))
#> Error : some focal IDs were removed from the store earlier and cannot be added again: a3
